channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Neutrophil RAGE drives early cerebrovascular injury after subarachnoid hemorrhage
item.description: An international research team from Japan and the United States, led by Assistant Professor Hiroshi Ishii and Professor Osamu Hori, together with Professors Yasuhiko Yamamoto and Mitsutoshi Nakada of Kanazawa University, has identified neutrophil RAGE (receptor for advanced glycation end products) as a key driver of early cerebrovascular injury after subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

item.title: Congo's Ebola deaths top 5,000 as fear of continent-wide spread mounts
item.description: Deaths in Congo's Ebola outbreak have topped 5,000 as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease and cases are recorded in other African countries, the latest government data on Saturday shows.

item.title: Treatment with norrin helps maintain healthy blood vessels and preserve vision in diabetic rats
item.description: Millions of people in the U.S. are affected by diabetic retinopathy, a complication of diabetes that affects the eyes. The condition is caused by damage to the blood vessels in the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. At first, diabetic retinopathy might not cause any symptoms, or the problems might be mild. However, if the underlying diabetes remains poorly managed, it can lead to blindness.

item.title: Personalized score uses ten blood markers to flag disease risk and assess healthy aging
item.description: Studies conducted in various countries indicate that approximately 60% of people over age 65 currently live with two or more chronic conditions. With the aim of reversing this trend and promoting healthy aging, European researchers have created a new personalized indicator that provides a detailed snapshot of a patient's metabolism by analyzing, with high precision, the chemicals the body produces to function.

item.title: New swab test could spare some women a painful biopsy for endometrial cancer
item.description: A simple vaginal swab may one day help women with abnormal bleeding learn whether they have endometrial cancer without first going through a painful biopsy.

item.title: Acute kidney injury up for older patients, men with OD-involved hospitalization
item.description: Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs more often among older patients and men with drug overdose–involved hospitalizations, while severe inpatient courses disproportionately affect younger patients, according to research published in the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

item.title: Patients with psoriasis have increased risks for cataracts, cataract surgery
item.description: Patients with psoriasis have an increased risk for cataracts and cataract surgery, with the risks for these outcomes varying by treatment modality, according to a study published online Oct. 26 in the Journal of Dermatology.

item.title: Living alone riskier for young and middle-aged adults than seniors, study indicates
item.description: Loneliness has been considered a major health risk for seniors, but a new study suggests younger adults might fare even worse from living by themselves. Living alone appears to increase a person's risk of death from a multitude of causes, particularly among adults 18 to 64, researchers reported in the International Journal of Epidemiology.

item.title: As a historic measles outbreak hits Pennsylvania Amish country, more show openness to vaccines
item.description: Amish and Mennonite shoppers in conservative dress mingled with shoppers from the wider public on a recent Friday at a vast outdoor market here, where vendors sold colorful pumpkins and mums, fry pies and squash, sports jerseys and Barbie accessories.

item.title: 7 predictors of renal dysfunction identified in patients with IBD
item.description: For patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), predictors of renal dysfunction have been identified and include osteoporosis, enteral nutrition, and intestinal surgery, according to a study published in BMC Gastroenterology.

item.title: How one of the body's own proteins drives the vicious cycle of inflammation in vaginal yeast infections
item.description: Up to three-quarters of all women will experience a genital yeast infection at least once in their lives. Recurrent infections, in particular, can significantly impair quality of life. The typical symptoms—such as itching, burning, and pain—are caused not only by the yeast Candida albicans, but, more importantly, by an excessive immune response. But why is the immune reaction in these cases so intense and persistent? An international research team led by the Leibniz-HKI has now uncovered how the host protein albumin fuels the inflammatory cascade while simultaneously shielding the fungal pathogen from the immune system. The findings have been published in Nature Communications.

item.title: Surgical recurrence less frequent with laparoscopic surgery for Crohn disease
item.description: For patients undergoing elective intestinal resection for Crohn disease (CD), cumulative surgical recurrence rates are lower with laparoscopic versus open surgery, according to a study published online July 23 in Techniques in Coloproctology.

item.title: Space-grown glioblastoma organoids could help advance brain cancer treatments
item.description: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults and is one of the most aggressive and deadly forms of cancer. It is difficult for surgeons to fully remove GBM because it often has microscopic "tentacles" that extend from the tumor into healthy brain tissue. GBM is also hard to treat because it creates an immunosuppressive microenvironment that helps the cancer evade immune attack and resist therapy.

item.title: Not all antihistamines are the same—and some may affect your brain more than you think
item.description: Millions of people take antihistamines for allergies, but some of these medicines can make you sleepy, slow your reactions and affect your concentration. Others are much less likely to have these effects. Knowing the difference can help you choose an allergy treatment that won't interfere with your day.

item.title: Human skin models reveal how herpes spreads unevenly among neighboring cells
item.description: Researchers at the Max Delbrück Center and University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf have traced how herpes simplex virus 1 infection progresses among neighboring skin cells in skin organoids. The work is published in Science Advances.

item.title: Team publishes largest-ever dataset on real-world psychedelic support interactions
item.description: "The Fireside Database: Large-Scale Evidence from 25,419 Psychedelic Support Interactions," published in Science Advances, provides researchers and policymakers with an empirical window into psychedelic use and support outside clinical settings.

item.title: Can creatine help your mental health? Here's what the latest evidence says
item.description: Once a supplement favored mainly by fitness fanatics, creatine has quickly become one of the most widely used dietary add-ons in the world.

item.title: Post-COVID syndrome: Prednisolone shows modest, short-lived lift in treatment trial
item.description: Persistent fatigue, shortness of breath, difficulty concentrating, anxiety or low mood: Many people continue to suffer from symptoms months after a COVID-19 infection, significantly restricting their daily lives. However, reliable data on which treatments are effective remain scarce.

item.title: First patient undergoes pioneering stem-cell treatment for Parkinson's
item.description: A patient has undergone pioneering stem-cell therapy to treat Parkinson's disease, the Japanese drugmaker behind the treatment said on Friday, in a world first following its conditional approval in the country.

item.title: Checkpoint immunotherapy reshapes immune environment in lymph nodes after melanoma reaches them
item.description: A new study from Mayo Clinic suggests checkpoint immunotherapy may reshape the immune environment within lymph nodes after melanoma has spread to them. Researchers found that treatment reorganized several types of immune cells and changed the behavior of certain cells, called macrophages, that can either support or suppress an immune response depending on their environment.

item.title: A rare case of Parkinson's disease reveals molecular changes in platelets during disease progression
item.description: A team from the Genomics and Transcriptomics of Synucleinopathies (GTS) research group at the Germans Trias i Pujol Research Institute (IGTP) has identified molecular changes in platelets associated with the progression of a rare case of early-onset Parkinson's disease. The study, published in Movement Disorders, highlights the value of these blood components as an accessible source for investigating potential biomarkers of disease progression.

item.title: Breast cancer drug raises creatinine without necessarily signaling kidney damage, study finds
item.description: A routine blood test can make a kidney look like it is failing when it is not. A team from Kanazawa University and Shinshu University has shown that this happens often in patients with breast cancer who take abemaciclib, and that a simple baseline measurement can help doctors tell the difference.

item.title: How mental health and cancer survivorship intersect
item.description: A Stanford Medicine study identified an often-overlooked period of vulnerability for cancer survivors: Mental health disorders identified two to five years after a cancer diagnosis were associated with a 119% higher rate of death from cancer compared with patients without documented mental disorders during the same period.

item.title: New treatment reduces heart scarring and abnormal heart rhythms, offering a possibility for future therapies
item.description: In a study led by Baylor College of Medicine and the University of Oxford, researchers found that blocking a specific molecular interaction reduced atrial fibrosis in mouse models and cells from human patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), reduced fibrotic responses in human cells, and in the mouse models reversed established atrial fibrosis and reduced abnormal heart rhythms.

item.title: Why some patients quit a newer insomnia medication
item.description: Researchers from Rutgers and other universities analyzed hundreds of online reviews on lemborexant—and learned that about 1 in 4 of the reviewers stopped or planned to stop taking the prescription medication used to treat insomnia.

item.title: Study reveals how congenital anomalies and deprivation impact children's educational achievement
item.description: New Welsh research has revealed how the combination of congenital anomalies, socioeconomic deprivation and other aspects of children's health and educational circumstances influences their attainment.

item.title: Platelets may play an unexpected role in glioblastoma progression
item.description: New Cleveland Clinic research published in Cancer Cell shows that people with glioblastoma have more active platelets, which are cells involved in blood clotting. Platelets also communicate with other cells and can influence immune activity. The overactive platelets in people with glioblastoma slow the activity of cancer-fighting T cells, which can contribute to tumor growth and cancer progression.

item.title: Alcohol use held steady among cancer survivors
item.description: The drinking rate of adults who have had cancer has remained unchanged for nearly a decade, according to a new study by researchers at the WashU Brown School.

item.title: Beyond treating symptoms: Life stories support mental health recovery
item.description: UT research shows how personal life stories can support treatment and personal recovery. Who are you, what has shaped you, and how do you see your future? For people with personality disorders, these questions can play an important role in their recovery. Ph.D. research by clinical psychologist and psychotherapist Silvia Pol shows that paying attention to personal life stories can help guide treatment decisions and support personal recovery.

item.title: Safer solutions: The urgent connection between smoking and HIV
item.description: People with HIV now lose more years of life to smoking than to HIV itself. About 1.2 million Americans are living with HIV, and while smoking among U.S. adults has fallen below 10% for the first time, people with HIV still smoke at up to four times that rate. Although many people with HIV want to quit smoking, their quit rates are much lower compared to the general population.
